questions.title: Why is a ternary weight set $\{-1,0,1\}$ described as 1.58 bits instead of 2 bits?
questions.question_body: In the paper "The Era of 1-bit LLMs", BitNet b1.58 uses weights in $\{-1,0,1\}$ and says that adding $0$ "results in 1.58 bits in the binary system". I thought three states usually need 2 bits to store if encoded directly. Is the 1.58 number just $\log_2 3$, meaning an information-theoretic lower bound, or do they actually pack weights so the average storage is close to 1.58 bits? I am confused about whether this is a theoretical naming convention or an actual implementation detail.

questions.title: If BitNet b1.58 uses 8-bit activations and full-precision embeddings, in what sense is it a "1-bit LLM"?
questions.question_body: The paper repeatedly calls BitNet b1.58 a "1-bit LLM", but later it says the model is trained with 1.58-bit weights and 8-bit activations, and it also mentions that embeddings remain full precision when discussing memory trends. Should I interpret "1-bit LLM" as referring only to the linear-layer weights, since those dominate the parameter count and compute? Or is there a more precise definition being used in low-bit LLM papers?

questions.title: How does the absmean quantization rule decide whether a weight becomes $-1$, $0$, or $1$?
questions.question_body: The paper defines quantization as $\widetilde{W} = \mathrm{RoundClip}(W/(\gamma + \epsilon), -1, 1)$ with $\gamma = \frac{1}{nm}\sum_{ij}|W_{ij}|$. If I understand correctly, after scaling, values in roughly $[-0.5, 0.5)$ are rounded to $0$, larger positive values go to $1$, and larger negative values go to $-1$, with clipping for very large magnitudes. Is that the right interpretation? If so, is the threshold at $\pm 0.5(\gamma + \epsilon)$ the main thing deciding sparsity?

questions.title: Why use the mean absolute value $\gamma = \frac{1}{nm}\sum_{ij}|W_{ij}|$ as the quantization scale?
questions.question_body: In BitNet b1.58, each weight matrix is divided by its average absolute value before rounding to $\{-1,0,1\}$. I can see how this normalizes the matrix, but I do not understand why the mean absolute value is preferred over something like the maximum absolute value, standard deviation, or a learned scale parameter. Is there an intuition for why absmean works especially well for ternary weights?

questions.title: How can matrix multiplication with ternary weights require almost no multiplications?
questions.question_body: The paper says BitNet b1.58 changes the computation paradigm and that matrix multiplication "requires almost no multiplication operations". But the model still multiplies ternary weights by 8-bit activations. Is the idea that multiplying by $-1$, $0$, or $1$ can be replaced by sign flips, skips, and additions? If so, does this only become true on custom hardware, or can current GPUs also avoid most multiply instructions in practice?

questions.title: What exactly does the paper mean by "feature filtering" from the extra $0$ weight value?
questions.question_body: One claimed advantage over the original binary BitNet is that ternary weights explicitly support "feature filtering" because a weight can be $0$. I am not sure how to interpret that. Does a zero weight act like a learned gate that suppresses certain input channels, or is it more like unstructured sparsity? Why would adding the option of $0$ improve modeling ability so much compared with forcing every connection to be either $-1$ or $1$?

questions.title: How are gradients computed through the non-differentiable rounding step in BitNet b1.58?
questions.question_body: The quantization function includes a rounding operation, which is not differentiable in the usual sense. The paper says BitNet b1.58 is trained from scratch, but in the excerpt I read it does not explain how optimization works through $\mathrm{round}(\cdot)$. Are they maintaining full-precision latent weights and using a straight-through estimator during backpropagation, as in some quantization-aware training methods? Or is there some different trick inherited from the original BitNet paper?

questions.title: Why does scaling activations to $[-Q_b, Q_b]$ remove the zero-point in quantization?
questions.question_body: The paper says that, unlike the original BitNet, activations are scaled per token to $[-Q_b, Q_b]$ "to get rid of the zero-point quantization". I am confused about this statement. In symmetric quantization, zero is often represented exactly anyway, so what zero-point are they avoiding here? Also, since some activations go through non-linearities like SwiGLU, why is symmetric per-token scaling still convenient?

questions.title: What does it mean that BitNet b1.58 "matches" FP16 starting from 3B parameters?
questions.question_body: The paper says BitNet b1.58 matches the FP16 LLaMA-like baseline starting from 3B model size, using the same training tokens. I am unsure how to interpret "matches" here. Does it mean statistically indistinguishable perplexity, similar average zero-shot accuracy, or just that the gap becomes small enough to be practically irrelevant? I am also wondering whether the main story is that quantization hurts small models more than large models, which would imply a different scaling behavior rather than simple parity.

questions.title: Why do the memory savings and latency speedups improve as the model size increases?
questions.question_body: The paper reports that BitNet b1.58 becomes relatively faster and more memory efficient at larger scales, for example reaching a $4.1\times$ speedup at 70B. The explanation mentions that the time cost of linear layers grows with model size and that embeddings remain full precision, so their fraction of total memory shrinks. Could someone explain this more concretely? Is the trend mainly because quantized linear layers dominate larger models, while the unquantized components become a smaller percentage of the total?

questions.title: Why are the embeddings kept in full precision if the paper says every parameter is ternary?
questions.question_body: Early in the paper, BitNet b1.58 is described as a model where "every single parameter (or weight)" is ternary in $\{-1,0,1\}$. Later, the memory discussion says that the embedding remains full precision, and that this is why its memory share matters less in larger models. Am I misunderstanding the scope of the ternary claim? Are token embeddings excluded from the "every parameter" statement, or is the implementation used for benchmarking slightly different from the conceptual model?

questions.title: How is the reported $71.4\times$ energy reduction calculated, and what is being excluded?
questions.question_body: The paper states that BitNet b1.58 saves $71.4\times$ arithmetic operations energy consumption for matrix multiplication on 7nm chips, based on prior energy models. I am trying to understand what exactly is counted in this number. Does it only compare the energy of FP16 multiply-adds against INT8 additions inside the matrix multiplications, while ignoring memory traffic, control overhead, softmax, normalization, and embedding lookups? If so, how should I relate that number to the smaller end-to-end energy gains reported later?

questions.title: What exactly is the "new scaling law" claimed for 1.58-bit LLMs?
questions.question_body: The paper says BitNet b1.58 enables a "new scaling law" and then gives examples like 13B BitNet b1.58 being more efficient than a 3B FP16 model in latency, memory, and energy. I am confused because this sounds more like an empirical tradeoff curve than a formal scaling law of the usual kind. Is there an actual functional relationship being proposed between model size, training tokens, performance, and inference cost, or is "scaling law" being used loosely to mean that larger ternary models can dominate smaller full-precision ones under a fixed cost budget?

questions.title: Does reducing activations from 16 bits to 8 bits really double the maximum context length?
questions.question_body: In the discussion section, the paper says BitNet b1.58 moves activations from 16 bits to 8 bits and therefore can double the context length under the same resources because of KV cache savings. I am not sure this follows automatically. KV cache memory is only one part of inference memory, and the cache stores keys and values rather than every intermediate activation. Is the doubling claim only approximately true when KV cache is the dominant memory cost, or is there some stronger argument?

questions.title: Is the claim of Pareto improvement fair when comparing BitNet b1.58 3.9B against an FP16 3B model?
questions.question_body: The paper says BitNet b1.58 3.9B is a Pareto improvement over a 3B FP16 LLaMA-like model because it is faster, uses less memory, and performs better. I understand the practical point, but I am unsure about the comparison methodology. Since the BitNet model has more parameters, should I think of this as "under a fixed deployment budget, I can afford a larger ternary model", rather than a direct apples-to-apples architecture comparison? I want to make sure I am interpreting the Pareto claim correctly.
